title: The High Price of Ownership
coreMove: Ask what you would pay for the thing today before ownership makes its loss feel larger than its use.
sourcePressure: The source explains the endowment effect: owning something inflates its value, makes selling feel like a loss, and turns labor or customization into attachment.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The weak version says people love their stuff; the precise lesson is that ownership changes the valuation question from use value to felt loss.

counterintuition: You know what it is worth
tryThisNow: Ask what you would pay today

exampleSpecs.domain: ceramic artist pricing a flawed kiln piece
exampleSpecs.audience: a maker deciding whether to list or keep a vase she spent weeks glazing
exampleSpecs.stakes: overpricing a flawed piece because labor and ownership feel like market value
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the artist covers her initials on the base and asks what she would pay if another maker brought the same warped vase to the table
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a blue-glazed vase with a warped rim cooling on a kiln shelf

exampleSpecs.domain: season-ticket holder pricing a single playoff seat
exampleSpecs.audience: a fan deciding whether to sell a ticket after years on a waiting list
exampleSpecs.stakes: demanding a price no buyer would pay because giving up the seat feels personal
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: a friend asks the fan to name the maximum he would pay today if the ticket were not already in his account
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a playoff ticket barcode glowing on a cracked phone screen

exampleSpecs.domain: family recipe blog considering deletion of low-traffic posts
exampleSpecs.audience: a blogger deciding whether to remove recipes that took years to photograph
exampleSpecs.stakes: protecting dead pages because the work invested makes them feel too valuable to cut
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the blogger compares traffic and remake requests after hiding author photos, then chooses which posts deserve the homepage
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a spreadsheet of page views beside stained handwritten recipe cards

exampleSpecs.domain: research lab deciding whether to retire a custom apparatus
exampleSpecs.audience: a principal investigator attached to a device built by former students
exampleSpecs.stakes: keeping unreliable equipment because ownership and history inflate its practical worth
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the lab covers the engraved build plaque and prices the apparatus as if it appeared used from another lab
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an aluminum apparatus with an engraved plaque under a dust cover

exampleSpecs.domain: vintage map dealer evaluating inherited stock
exampleSpecs.audience: a dealer who inherited unsold maps from a mentor
exampleSpecs.stakes: setting prices from attachment instead of actual buyer demand
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the dealer turns the mentor's notes facedown and sorts the maps by recent comparable sales before assigning prices
exampleSpecs.firstImage: rolled maps tied with cotton tape across a green felt counter

exampleSpecs.domain: restaurant owner selling a hand-painted sign after rebranding
exampleSpecs.audience: an owner deciding what the old sign is worth to another business
exampleSpecs.stakes: confusing memory of opening night with what the sign can earn now
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after photographing the sign without the storefront behind it, the owner writes what a stranger could use it for and lowers the asking price
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a hand-painted sign leaning against a brick wall before sunrise

skillTargets: spot endowment effect in pricing and retention
distinguish use value from loss feeling
evaluate when customization or labor is inflating valuation

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one thing you own but rarely use; hide the ownership cue and write the most you would pay to buy it today from a stranger.
